  convolutional networks to map low-resolution (LR) videos to high-resolution
  (HR) videos.  Although this approach has shown great success, the assumption
  that local convolutional patterns remain consistent across scales limits the

  that utilizes a spatial attention mechanism to identify salient regions in the
  LR video and corresponding LR-to-HR mapping offsets.  These components then
  enable a hypothesis-driven volume traversal module at a high resolution to
  locate the corresponding region in the HR video and guide the traversal at
  a lower resolution to reduce unnecessary computations.  Furthermore, our ABNet
  achieves superior results by integrating prior knowledge from the LR video
  computation into the HR video computation, thereby also addressing the assumption
  of joint computation.  Comprehensive experiments on standard video super-resolution
  datasets demonstrate that our ABNet significantly outperforms the baseline
  convolutional network and achieves superior quantitative and visual results.

Considering a (2+1)-dimensional topological insulator coupled to an even-dimensional Chern-Simons response at (3+1)-dimensional surface, we investigate the interplay between Weyl and anomaly transport within this configuration.  First, we describe the Chern-Sim response within a (2+1)-dimensional edge state using a non-Abelian K-matrix model and subsequently calculate both the Weyl and anomaly transport coefficients. A key aspect of this endeavor is developing efficient algorithms to perform basic tensor operations, including calculations of Kronecker products, sums, and linear transformations based on structured sparse representations of tensors. Although significant progress has been made in this area for binary tensors, similar progress for complex tensors lags behind. This paper introduces structured representations for certain classes of complex sparse tensors and develops efficient algorithms for performing fundamental tensor operations using these structures. Specifically, we present two representations for the sparse unitary Fourier transform of a complex sparse tensor and provide corresponding algorithms to perform these transformations. We also derive conditions for the Kronecker product and tensor sum of structured sparse tensors and propose a general method for identifying the structured sparse representation for their results. However, the presence of a component that operates only in one direction introduces nonlinearity, which is common in applications such as electrical diodes and optical modulators.  Since this type of behavior can be represented by a piecewise linear function, it is useful to develop a general framework for mechanical vibrations with unilateral components.  This paper derives a variational principle based on the minimization of the convex hull of an non-convex, lower semi-continuous quadratic form, specifically used to describe the convexification process of the damping component.  It is shown that this problem is equivalent to the underlying piecewise linear differential equation, and a uniqueness theorem is proven for the solution.  Additionally, it is demonstrated that the problem can be reduced to the convex hull minimization of the associated Hessian form.  The results obtained in this study are applicable to a broader range of systems, including those containing a general nonlinear component that operates unidirectionally, and it is believed that the framework established here can be utilized to describe systems in mechanics, electrical circuits, and optical applications.

As such, there has been significant research into developing efficient methods for annotating objects on images by automatically suggesting plausible bounding boxes for models to approve or adjust.  While there are many models that suggest plausible annotations, they often fail to provide accurate predictions of the annotations' categories.  To address this shortcoming, we developed a method for efficient image annotation based on a novel, lightweight network called the Efficient Suggestion Network (ESN).  The ESN is trained to suggest plausible bounding boxes for each image, along with their correct category labels.  The ESN achieves this performance through efficient use of annotations from existing datasets, a targeted loss function, and an optimal architecture.  Our method is particularly effective when compared to other models, as it is able to suggest accurate plausible annotations with the right loss function and an optimal architecture.  The ESN is also robust across multiple architectures and methods for pre-training and fine-tuning.  Our experimental results show that the ESN is able to suggest accurate plausible annotations in a model-agnostic manner, along with their correct category labels.  The ESN is also shown to be effective in suggesting annotations on images that are not part of its training set.  Furthermore, training and testing E(object) object proposals and suggestions are shown to be effective in enhancing the performance of existing object detection models.

Adversarial Networks
  (GANs) can excel at image generation tasks.  However, the mathematical
  incomprehensibility of the adversarial training process hinders the
  development of theoretical knowledge about GANs.  This paper introduces a
  fresh perspective on multilayer perceptron-based adversarial models,
  illustrating that the optimal solution to this class of models can be
  expressed in a closed-form equation.  According to this formula, each
  intermediate node in the multilayer perceptron network either contributes
  to defining an optimal solution to a generative task or is superfluous. This
  discovery enables a more efficient multilayer perceptron configuration,
  potentially leading to faster training and enhanced solution quality. This
  research also paves the way for additional multilayer perceptron-based
  investigations into generative tasks.

Wi-Fi-based positioning systems are becoming a key area of focus.  This study presents an efficient and precise indoor localization method using a combination of 6G technology and machine learning, specifically targeting the limitations of traditional Wi-Fi positioning systems.  To tackle the challenge of high dimensionality in 6D data, a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network is utilized to extract meaningful temporal patterns before employing a Support Vector Regression model for accurate position prediction.  To validate the effectiveness of this approach, a unique 6D dataset is collected experimentally and the results demonstrate a high level of prediction accuracy with low root mean square error values.  To further enhance the performance of the proposed method, a set of optimization techniques are suggested and the best configuration yields exceptional outcomes with a highly efficient prediction accuracy and low error value.  To accelerate the prediction process, a parallel processing approach on a 6G processor is also explored and the results indicate a high level of processing speed and accuracy. Overall, this research presents a novel and effective approach to precise real-time indoor localization using 6D data, with the potential to meet the requirements of 6G technology.

) is a method that identifies valuable insights from a dataset while accounting for the uncertainty of the findings. This uncertainty arises due to the unavailability of the underlying data distribution and any data preprocessing steps taken. To address this, a new dataset preprocessing and analysis framework called Robust Learning from Data (RLFD) has been developed which gives due consideration to the uncertainty introduced by its own decisions, such as processing and preprocessing choices and processing data via a particular learning algorithm. To demonstrate the framework's capabilities, a specific learning algorithm known as Probabilistic Law Discovery (PLD) has been developed and integrated into the framework. The PLD algorithm detects patterns within the data that yield optimal results for a given objective function, and which are likely to occur in other datasets drawn from the same distribution. The RLFD framework then presents and compares the discovered patterns along with their uncertainty measures in a unified format. Together, the framework and the PLD algorithm can process and analyze datasets in a coherent and consistent manner which takes into account the uncertainty introduced by its own processes.

We compared the code's predictions with 21-cm absorption data for four of these galaxies using the REDDION radio telescope and a future deep field survey. Results. $\alpha$ decay properties of $^{210}$Po have long served as a benchmark for theoretical models of $p$-hole systems near closed shells. Despite being well-studied, accurately calculating its decay energy still poses significant challenges. This study aims to address this difficulty by employing the extended Shell Model with Quasiparticles (QSMMfx) framework, utilizing four different Skyrme function sets to precisely compute its low-lying excitation energies and decay energies. Method: In this approach, both $\beta$ decay log ft values and $\alpha$ decay half-lives are calculated using unique axial deformation parameters ($\gamma$) and intrinsic states for $^{206}$Pb and $^{208}$Pb cores, respectively, which are specific to each nuclear reaction. Results: Our research demonstrates that utilizing reaction-specific intrinsic states yields a more accurate calculation of $\alpha$ decay half-lives, in contrast to the traditional method of using universal intrinsic states. The computed log ft values and experimental values show good overall agreement, with a slight underestimation trend. Similarly, the calculated $\alpha$ decay half-life is in reasonable accord with the experimental data, albeit with an order of magnitude discrepancy. Conclusion: The findings of this research suggest that the precise choice of deformation parameters and intrinsic states is of paramount importance in accurately predicting decay half-lives through the Quasiparticle Shell Model (QSMM) method.

However, these weak labels contain significantly more noise compared to precise point labels, necessitating the development of robust methods for semantic segmentation that can utilize weakly-annotated data efficiently. Current techniques for this purpose typically rely on the intersection over union (IoU) function, which has been mathematically proven to be non-suitable for directly optimizing the segmentation task due to its non-convex and non-smooth characteristics as a result of the maximum operation. The concept of deformation bursts was initially developed to describe noise generated by friction and later expanded to include phenomena such as acoustic emission and sonoluminescence.  The analysis of sequence statistical characteristics in rocks under uniaxial compression in a laboratory setting provides fresh perspective on understanding the connection between deformation bursts and understanding similar processes occurring in geological faults deep within the Earth's crust.  The study reveals that deformation bursts exhibit a scale-invariant distribution of sizes, which closely resembles characteristics found in natural systems, requiring the examination of additional statistical features to differentiate between geologically occurring processes. Existing code summarization methods primarily focus on learning code representations and utilizing them to generate summaries.  In this work, we take a different approach, viewing code summarization from the perspective of feature abstraction, where the goal is to identify general patterns that explain the code's purpose.  Building on this perspective, we first automatically extract code features from the given code, and then use these features to automatically produce a summary via feature selection and linear combination.  To accomplish this, we develop a novel graph-based code feature extraction method, involving the construction of a program dependence graph, its reduction to a dominance frontier graph, and the extraction of dominance frontier features.  Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art code summarization methods in both automatic evaluation, where we ask developers to rate the quality of existing approaches versus ours, and manual evaluation.  Furthermore, our approach demonstrates superior performance in code comprehension tasks.

F) in the human brain, gamma oscillations play a vital role in binding the other DoFs of spatial, temporal, and modal dimensions. Studies on gamma oscillations have primarily focused on their association with cognitive processes within the brain's local areas. However, their involvement in long-distance brain connections has been largely overlooked. Although recent advancements in technology have highlighted their potential in mapping long-distance brain connections, current methods face limitations such as subjectivity, lack of causality assessment, and individual variability. To address these challenges, we introduce GammaLink, a novel method for extracting gamma coherence features that incorporate gamma's dimensions of space, time, and mode, enabling a comprehensive characterization of long-distance brain connections. By integrating these features into a deep learning framework, we demonstrate the efficacy of gamma connections in predicting both regional and global brain network properties, such as small-worldness and modularity. Our experiments indicate the ability of gamma connections to explain up to 28% of the variance in small-worldness and 20% of the variance in modularity, thus establishing the role of gamma oscillations in shaping the brain network architecture.

growing interest in using 3D scene text recognition technology in various commercial applications, which requires a deep understanding of the underlying relationships between visual features and textual content.  Although current state-of-the-art methods have achieved notable success, they primarily rely on purely visual approaches that often fail to capture the complete picture.  As a consequence, these techniques are prone to overfitting to appearance patterns and struggle to distinguish between visually similar but textually different words.  To tackle this limitation, we propose a novel text-aware feature learning approach, which enables the model to automatically discover encodings that capture the semantic relationships between visual features and textual content.  Specifically, we introduce a text-aware feature learning network, which leverages an auxiliary text-aware objective function to guide the learning of text-aware feature representations.  To enhance the text-aware feature encodings, we incorporate an adversarial process, which alternately optimizes a text discriminator and an encoder network to produce text-aware feature representations that are difficult to distinguish.  As the result, our text-aware feature learning approach effectively learns encodings that capture the needed information for recognizing text while filtering out any extraneous visual patterns not related to the text's meaning.  To validate the efficacy of our approach, we conduct comprehensive experiments on three public datasets, which demonstrate that our text-aware feature learning network can significantly enhance scene text recognition performance by accurately capturing the relationship between visual features and textual content.

This attack allows the adversary to masquerade as multiple legitimate devices and launch coordinated attacks, thereby increasing their chances of success in compromising the grid's security protocols.  To assess the impact of such an attack, we built a testbed that replicates a secure communication protocol used in power grid systems, based on 802.11ah and developed a simulation model to predict its consequences.  Our results show that by disrupting the communication security protocol, the adversary can paralyze the entire system, leaving it vulnerable and unable to transmit data, thereby causing significant operational disruptions.  To mitigate the impact of such an attack, we propose a new authentication protocol based on IPsec, which limits the scope of the attack and forces the system to revert to normal operation even when some devices have been compromised.  Our evaluation of this protocol reveals that it can contain the attack within a single network segment, limiting its impact to approximately 10% of the system.

Instead, we propose a novel method that leverages the full Fisher Information Matrix to identify and prune the least informative components that would have the least impact on the model's generalization performance.  Our experiments on diverse models and datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in achieving more accurate sub-net models with significantly fewer parameters compared to the state-of-the-art methods.  Additionally, the pruning results for large models in the proposed work exceed the accuracy of some recently proposed knowledge distillation techniques.

  Although many works have addressed graphically structured Bayesian models,
  their sparse solutions often lead to models with numerous superfluous associations. In
  contrast, our proposed Bayesian approach, aimed at achieving a more complete and
  interpretable representation of relationships within data, yields a dense solution.
  Our method builds upon a previously established dense Bayesian model for undirected
  conditional independence, adapting it for spatially correlated variables via an
  innovative extension of a customised kernel function to an undirected graphical model.
  While this approach is grounded in a well-established and mathematically sound
  framework, its application to large-scale spatial data sets poses significant
  computational challenges due to its dense nature. To mitigate this, we developed an
  innovative two-stage variational inference procedure that efficiently fits the model
  to substantial spatial data sets. Specifically, we first fit a sparse approximation
  of the model and then pruned its precision matrix using a bespoke kernel-based
  approximation of its inverse, allowing us to obtain a dense solution while retaining
  computational benefits of a sparse model. Our approach is supported by rigorous
  theoretical guarantees, including convergence rates and optimal approximation
  properties, and includes extensions to related models such as Gaussian processes
  regression with spatial covariates and Markov random fields.

algorithm for quantum states, the qLZ77 algorithm.  The proposed method mimics the classic Lossless-Ziv-Lempel (LZ77) algorithm but is tailored for compressing periodic periodic quantum states efficiently.  The algorithm analyzes the sliding window for the best match of a given quantum state block and constructs the best match pair consisting of a longest match length and an offset. creating nontrivial topological phases in condensed matter physics.  However, some systems with high symmetry don't necessitate symmetry breaking to exhibit topological properties.  Such topological phases can arise from quantum entanglement among degenerate many-body states, resulting in nontrivial topology without any symmetry breaking.  This phenomenon is called "self-topological phase".  Previously reported self-topological phases are limited to few-dimensional systems with degenerate ground states that form geometrically localized ground-state manifolds.  In this study, we introduce a self-topological phase in the many-dimensional Hilbert space of the spin-1 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a kagome lattice.  When next-nearest-neighbor interactions exceed a certain threshold, the system's ground-state degeneracy exhibits nontrivial topology in the many-dimensional Hilbert space.  This result indicates that high-dimensional self-topological phases can emerge from frustrated systems without requiring geometrically localized ground-state manifolds.

However, an investigation at the interface between small and large scale magnetic fields discovered that the Parker-Neumann instability can cause the amplification of the magnetic field, regardless of initial conditions, as long as there is a sufficient contrast in the component perpendicular to the magnetic field lines. to overcome the limitations of independent play by allowing the outcome of one game to influence another.  This study delves into the consequences of dependence on game outcomes, considering various forms of complete dependence and their impact on players' winnings.  The results reveal unexpected phenomena, including situations where two losing games become winning when played in dependence, and surprising winner/loser combinations can emerge from independently playing identical games.  The dependence required to change the results from losing to winning or from winning to losing is quantified and compared.  The influence of games played in dependence is examined using complete pairwise dependence models.  A key finding is the discovery of a threshold effect, demonstrating that the more games played simultaneously, the less dependent the games need to be to transform the players' winnings.  This is followed by an introduction to games played in random dependence and analysis of completely pairwise dependent games.  A general rule is established that the more games played simultaneously, the less dependent they need to be, based on the formula $1/N$, where $N$ is the number of games played simultaneously.  This study has significant implications for Parrondo games in contexts such as financial markets, where complete independence may not be the most realistic assumption.

alo connection, dark matter halos are often substituted with "proxy" objects to streamline post-processing steps.  We introduce a novel approach by demonstrating that a specific subset of a halos' stellar content can directly serve as a suitable substitute.  By analyzing the relationship between a halos' total mass and the counts of a specific proxy object, we show that the proxy's properties are determined by the halo's mass alone, thus satisfying the closure assumption.  As an illustration, we employ the number of galaxies in group 3 and higher, identified through the SDSS's group catalog, as our proxy.  Using proxy-based analysis, we recover established results from prior literature, including the halo-halo mass function, the concentration-mass relation, the stellar mass function, and the galaxy-halo bias.  Crucially, our method yields an alternative estimation of galaxy formation efficiency that is consistent with prior research, yet is 2-3 times more precise.  Our study provides a novel, streamlined, and highly efficient framework for evaluating and constraining semi-analytical models and simulations of galaxy formation, with significant computational advantages, particularly when employing large-scale proxy samples.

ube technique is a widely-used approach in medical imaging, particularly in tracing and tracking the contours of anatomical structures. Although the basic principle behind this method is straightforward to implement, the complexity arises from designing a suitable distance function that accurately captures the curvature of the target object. While numerous techniques have been developed for contour tracking based on the minimization of potential energy, the application of the Geodesic Regression framework in this domain has yet to be explored. In our study, we introduce a groundbreaking approach that utilizes a simple potential function and iteratively solves the geodesic PDE to adjust the contour in response to curvature. Additionally, we present an efficient algorithm for solving the inverse problem of finding the initial condition of a level set that generates a given object, and apply it to contour tracking. The proposed solution involves a regularized backward heat equation, solved using an adaptive time step technique. Our findings indicate that the new approach converges rapidly, provides multiple local minimum solutions, and can successfully track contours in the presence of noise.

has proven effective in generating high-quality actions and solving complex control problems.  Nevertheless, a significant challenge lies in formulating reward functions that accurately reflect real-world consequences, particularly in robotics where direct experimentation is costly.  Although learning reward functions from observations has been extensively studied, the process is hindered by the credit assignment problem, where pinpointing the source of a delayed and aggregated reward from multiple observations is difficult.  To overcome this obstacle, our approach treats learning a reward function from observation and action data as a reverse reinforcement learning problem, where we develop a policy to maximize the likelihood of observed rewards given past observations and actions.  Drawing inspiration from successful reinforcement learning algorithms, we adapt the Actor-Critic framework, where an actor policy learns to anticipate rewards based on observations, and a critic function estimates the likelihood of observed rewards given the actor's actions and the actual rewards received.  By training this actor-critic system on simulated data, we successfully learn a discriminative model that captures the underlying relationship between actions, observations, and rewards.  Then, using this learned reward model, we demonstrate its effectiveness in predicting the outcome of hypothetical scenarios and fine-tuning agents in real-world settings.  Our research highlights the potential of this approach in scenarios involving delayed and aggregated rewards, and paves the way for more efficient and accurate learning algorithms in robotics and other applications.

  problem is largely due to the limited availability of training data that

  negatives when predicting rare events.  This issue is particularly evident in
  applications like earthquake forecasting, flood anticipation, and disease
  outbreak prediction.  Current evaluation metrics used in the field of time
  series classification tend to prioritize accurate predictions around labeled
  training samples rather than capturing the difficulty of forecasting rare
  events.  This research proposes a new approach to time series classification
  that centers on predicting upcoming anomalies rather than general anomalies.
  It introduces a comprehensive evaluation framework known as AUPR-Forecasting
  (AUC of Positive Recall for Forecasting) to measure a model's ability to
  generate high positive recalls during rare events.  Through thorough analysis
  and extensive experimentation on real-world datasets for earthquake prediction,
  flood anticipation, and outbreak forecasting, it demonstrates that existing
  deep learning models struggle to generate high positive recalls during rare
  events and that the AUPR-Forecasting evaluation framework effectively
  pinpoints this deficiency.  It is argued that the development of models
  capable of accurately predicting future anomalies is crucial for developing
  reliable deep learning-based time series classification models.

We prove that delayed Bell nonlocality and delayed quantum entanglement are equivalent and can be utilized to characterize their respective direct counterparts.  Specifically, a multi dice system exhibits Bell nonlocality or quantum entanglement if and only if its delayed system interacts directly or is quantumly entangled, implying that these direct relationships are delay-proof.  A practical test is developed to detect Bell nonlocality and quantum entanglement in a delayed dice roll system by analyzing its direct counter part.  Our study holds significance for understanding the fundamental nature of Bell nonlocality and quantum entanglement in complex, indirect interactions.

However, in multi-view reconstruction scenarios, these models often struggle with occlusions and inaccurate predictions on some views. In this work, we introduce a novel framework for robust multi-view reconstruction, called R3Rec, consisting of two key innovations: first, an innovative occlusion-aware network that enhances occluded regions in images that are not visible in other views, and second, an adaptive refinement module that selectively refulates predictions on views with high confidence and only corrects erroneous predictions on views with low confidence. Additionally, we propose a scheme that combines predictions from all views and adjusts the influence of each prediction based on its confidence. Our approach is straightforward to integrate into existing multi-view stereo systems and can be trained using the same multi-view data. Our approach has been shown to deliver superior results on standard benchmarks such as S3UM and KIT, and also performs well in real-world applications.

To address this issue, a growing interest has emerged in developing low-resource LMs that utilize knowledge from pre-trained large-scale models through knowledge distillation.  While this technique is commonly used, there's a lack of thorough investigation into the underlying mechanism of how the student model acquires knowledge from both the training data and the teacher model.  In this research, we use a combination of probe training and perturbation analysis to examine the knowledge composition and interplay within a student model.  Our study provides valuable insights into the inner workings of this knowledge distillation technique and has significant implications for understanding neural networks more broadly.  Based on our findings, we suggest potential strategies to manipulate the knowledge embedded in student models, which can be used to optimize the models for downstream tasks, shift their decision boundaries, and control the interplay between the learned knowledge and inserted pseudoknowledge.

The proximity of the human body, particularly the head, can significantly affect the antenna performance and the propagation of the signal. The integrated antenna uses a grounded L-shaped slot and achieves high gain through the use of shorting vias that improve the radiation efficiency. in interest, with machine learning (ML) models being employed to capture the intricate interactions between large eddies and small eddies that conventional Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) approaches fail to accurately represent.  By incorporating the empirical correlations derived from high-fidelity simulations into RANS frameworks, these models can potentially bridge the gap between the two extremes and yield more precise predictions of turbulent flows.  Nevertheless, the application of such models is hindered by a lack of consideration for uncertainty quantification (UQ), which is crucial for assessing the reliability of UQ and validating models.  In this study, we present an integrated UQ and validation framework that takes into account parameter uncertainty and modeling error in an effort to quantify the uncertainty of the model's predictions.  In our analysis, we incorporate process-based probability distributions to model the uncertainty of small-scale eddies' effects and employ a Kullback-Leibler divergence metric to evaluate the discrepancy between the model's predictions and the direct numerical simulation (DNS) data.  In order to address the high computational cost of UQ, we utilize the sparse grid Monte Carlo (sGMC) method to efficiently explore the uncertainty and validate the model.  In our UQ and validation analysis, we utilize a DNS database of channel flow at a Reynolds number of 1075 and apply the UQ and validation method to two data-driven turbulence closure models, demonstrating significant reductions in prediction uncertainty for both models.

When a metallic layer containing a supercurrent and an oxide containing reversed magnetization come into contact, the spin-Hall effect generates strong spin waves in the ferromagnetic material.  These spin waves modify the spin triplet component of the supercurrent, creating a resistance similar to that of the ordinary effect of the magnetization.  However, due to the spin-wave's dynamic nature, resistance fluctuations occur at a frequency matching the spin wave's precession frequency.  The research was performed on a system consisting of niobium and yttrium iron oxide, with the supercurrent flowing parallel to the magnetization.  A distinct peak in resistance oscillates at twice the fundamental precession frequency of the spin wave, when driven by the spin-Hall effect, and this peak persists even when the spin-Hall voltage exceeds the superconducting energy gap.

In contrast, data that naturally occurs in nature lacks labels, making passive data collection methods ineffective for gathering such comprehensive, labeled information. To address this challenge, we propose a deep active learning framework that employs unsupervised training on naturally occurring data in its environment to identify areas where labeling would have the most significant impact on model performance. By leveraging weak and strong augmentation techniques to determine which data to label, we demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in two distinct environments. Firstly, in an image-based setting, we target the most beneficial dog breed images for a ResNet-101 classifier, achieving comparable results to human annotators while reducing the number of annotated images by 90%. Secondly, in a language model setting, we aim to improve RoBERTa's performance with minimal active loss targets, outperforming strong baselines under a 10% active dataset size. Overall, our proposed framework paves the way for more efficient training of deep neural networks with naturally occurring, unlabeled data.

The Nambu-Goldstone theorem suggests that broken continuous symmetries should result in zero-eigenvalue modes, yet the non-invertible nature of $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry poses a significant challenge in this regard. To address this challenge, our research proposes a new paradigm for $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric systems by introducing a set of $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric sum rules that outline the boundary between $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric and asymptotic regions in parameter space. Leveraging the concept of pseudo-momentum, our analysis identifies a parity inversion point that marks the beginning of the broken $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric region and gives rise to a parity inversion wave at the boundary of the system, which is analogous to the nonexistence of Nambu-Goldstone modes. Through numerical simulations and diagonalization methods, we validate our theoretical findings, revealing the unique characteristics of $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric systems and their unique boundary phenomena.

in various astrophysical and terrestrial plasmas, researchers rely on a two-point correlation function to derive a quasi-linear turbulent diffusivity. health and mobility worldwide. The 9/11 attacks demonstrated the power of large-scale violence to shock the global community. As such, tracking changes in global search interest following these tragic events is essential for understanding their lasting impact. The study analyzes daily worldwide search trend data on various topics related to terrorism, COVID-19 symptoms, and health-related topics before and after 9/11 and March 11, 2020. The results revealed significant spikes in global search interest related to COVID-19 symptoms and health topics at the beginning of the pandemic. Similarly, following 9/11, there was a notable increase in global search interest related to terrorism and anthrax for a few weeks, followed by a shift in focus to other topics. However, following the anthrax attacks, there was a notable decrease in global search interest, underscoring the difference between events with visible casualties and those that take place out of the sight of the public.

Despite the fact that researchers who deploy these models are working to protect them, they can still be subject to potential threats. In an effort to protect the architecture and parameters of a pre-trained model, we propose a novel approach to obfuscating deep neural networks. Our approach transforms the original model into a functionally equivalent but larger and more complex equivalent model, making it challenging to reverse-engineer the original model's parameters through various analytical methods. probabilistic finite automata with fractional powers of $q$ as base is an ongoing investigation we expand upon.  Previous work by Kiefer and Th\'erien showed that determining whether an automaton represents a constant, polynomial, or exponential function depends on the complexity of the logarithm of $q$.  We enhance this understanding for exponential functions when $q$ is an integer or $1$, logging $q$ becomes trivial.  We show that any finite-state MPFA with integer $q$ power of $q$ as base, computes a polynomial if the degree of $Q$ is sufficiently low, specifically, $ \text{deg}(Q) \leqslant |Q| + |A| + |Q| \log_{q}|Q|$.  Additionally, we indicate that this threshold can be improved, but likely not beyond $ \text{deg}(Q) \leqslant |Q| + |A| + |Q| \log_{q}|Q|$.  We also discuss the feasibility of this threshold when $q$ equals one.

However, V2G participation may lead to an increase in vehicle range anxiety due to the use of grid electricity during driving. To address this concern, this study develops a V2G scheduling optimization model, which aims to maximize the economic value of grid electricity and vehicle range by strategically utilizing the vehicle's storage capacity. To understand the impact of DM's mass and intrinsic nature, we employ three distinct DM field theories. Concurrently, a set of four dark and Standard Model field theories are utilized to examine different mediator properties. To comprehensively approach the problem, we adopt the "front-end approach" by integrating a wide range of constraints from direct DM detection, collider experiments, and indirect searches. chemical systems is frequently influenced by their surrounding environment through a complex web of interactions. This relationship can manifest in various forms, from cooperative and mutual interactions to concurrent correlations and asynchronous connections. This dynamic system encompasses multiple inputs and outputs that are characterized by their synchronous and asynchronous nature, as well as their cooperative and competitive aspects. This data, often high-dimensional and continuously streaming, is essential for understanding system functionality and predicting future outcomes. This study focuses on constructing causal graphs from this data from the perspectives of both the system and the environment. These constructed models are based on the concepts of Synchronous Asynchronous Coupled Networks, which identify the direct causes from the combined internal system and external environment influences. This approach also incorporates the concept of Contextual Granger Causality to account for both internal and external system correlations. The results from this study are further validated through the examination of multiple synthetic and real-world datasets, covering datasets from biological, physical, and chemical applications, as well as from the electrical and mechanical industries. The findings are compared to non-contextual methods to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in accurately modeling the underlying processes from both the system and the environment perspectives.

The paper extends the double-well model to incorporate the trigonal Kerr effect within the framework of nonlinear density matrix theory, focusing specifically on pure states.  The addition of the trigonal term results in a state of increased complexity, with a level of intricacy that surpasses that of the square law. The study also explores the impact of the trigonal term on states of maximum coherence, as well as states of minimum uncertainty, in its theoretical analysis.

To achieve this, the BESHT employs a sophisticated set of techniques, including a wide-field corrector, a multi-band system, a high-stability structure, a precise pointing and tracking mechanism, a active thermal control system, and a 2k pixel CCD detector to ensure optimal performance and minimize noise.  After outlining BESHT's key features, we detail the results of its six-month operational trials, demonstrating that the system can effectively mitigate sources of noise, maintain signal stability, and achieve observational efficiencies of over 90%.  These advancements make BESHT capable of conducting multi-night observations and making faint detections, thus setting the stage for its capability to discover super-Earth and Neptune-sized exoplanets in the coming decade.

  A major challenge in reinforcement learning lies in effectively combining simulated and real-world datasets to train policy models.
  While recent research has focused on employing high-quality simulated data for improving the reinforcement learning policy, such data is often difficult to generate.

To counter this force, the rotation of a planet can generate a centrifugal barrier, keeping small dust grains from escaping, thus facilitating the build-up of a terrestrial planet. However, this phenomenon is only viable for highly spinning large bodies, which may not be a common feature of the early solar system. In an effort to overcome this limitation, we have investigated the accumulation of dust around the surface of rapidly spinning Earth-sized bodies in the phase model and have discovered that stable dust traps can form even in bodies rotating more than seven times faster than its critical limit. We observe the Na I D absorption in the interstellar medium along various sight lines, which enables us to reconstruct sodium distributions. We applied this technique to 167 low-latitude sight lines toward 42 quasars, analyzing a total of 167 Na measurements at a galactocentric distance greater than 10 kpc. We discovered a clear gradient in sodium abundance, with the outer regions exhibiting higher sodium concentrations compared to the galactic center. This phenomenon can be attributed to a process that transports gas outward from the center, likely driven by a negative slope in the radial pressure of the interstellar medium. We propose a model where a cold molecular gas disk, supported by rotation, becomes unstable to a process called "gravitational shear" which creates shear flows that transport the coldest and densest gas to the outer regions of the galaxy. We found this model to be consistent with our data, which we compare to predictions made by the GALSHEAR code. We also discovered that the "gravitational shear" instability is particularly effective at transporting cold molecular gas in the outer regions of galaxies, which may have implications for the formation of stars.

Despite their advantages, training BNNs remains computationally expensive and often infeasible at scale compared to conventional methods like distillation.  In this study, we introduce Learning to Distill (L2D), a novel approach that enables the training of neural networks through the simulation of distillation losses, which are designed to be both flexible and interpretable.  L2D leverages a virtual teacher network trained on synthetic data to generate soft targets for a student network to process.  By optimizing these losses, L2D can produce networks with performance on par with conventional overfit models, while also excelling in evaluation metrics such as maximum likelihood and uncertainty calibration.  Furthermore, L2D demonstrates the ability to distill complex models like ResNets and Vision Transformers, showcasing the versatility of our approach.

The time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) method, a popular approach for calculating molecular excitations, has been successfully applied with a range of functionals. However, using the long-range corrected (LRC) functionals in core electron excitations yields inconsistent results due to an issue known as the self-interaction error (SIE). This study investigates the origin of this failure by comparing two distinct SIE models, utilizing a sum-rule constraint to highlight an limitation of the adiabatic approximation that contributes to the SIE problem. It is concluded that the primary cause of the SIE failure in LRC functionals is actually a short-range issue, rather than an inability to model long-range interactions. This is further complicated by the fact that core orbitals have a high degree of localization, which can lead to numerical inaccuracies in exchange integrals. To validate this, H-Ly manometric dissociation was simulated, demonstrating that even when using an LRC functional that incorrectly models long-range interactions, the resulting spectrum is still inaccurate due to a short-range problem. This is in contrast to using a PBE functional, which results in a recoverable spectrum through an LRC functional correction, as the self-interaction error in this case is short-range in origin. This study emphasizes the need to carefully consider the nature of SIE when applying TD-DFT to molecular excitations.

These developments have significantly boosted the performance of agents in certain benchmark tasks within controlled environments. However, there has been a relative lack of progress in applying these techniques to more challenging problems beyond these benchmarks. As a result, the current generation of reinforcement learning algorithms tends to prioritize achieving high rewards over gathering a comprehensive understanding of their environment. This pursuit of extreme optimization may be limiting the ability of these algorithms to handle unforeseen events and adapt to new situations. In an effort to investigate the concept of "learning for robust generalization" within the realm of reinforcement learning, our research explores whether agents can develop a more holistic understanding of their environment while still maximizing their rewards. To do this, we introduce two new objectives for evaluating policy performance, centered on learning representations that capture a comprehensive view of the state space and facilitate efficient recovery of optimal policies in new tasks. We assess these objectives against existing reinforcement learning baselines and propose novel gradient-based methods for integrating reward exploration with environmental understanding. Our findings suggest that "learning for robust generalization" can enable agents to produce more diverse behavior, acquire more complete representations of their environment, and efficiently accomplish complex multi-step tasks.

  deterministic integration of deterministic structures is a key prerequisite
  for the development of quantum technologies. Deterministic placement of
  single defects in host materials is now well-established for 2D crystals, but
  achieving this determination for bulk semiconductors remains a significant
  challenge. Deterministic fabrication techniques for optical cavities have also
  made substantial progress in recent years, but combining deterministic
  defect generation with deterministic cavity fabrication in bulk semiconductors
  remains an outstanding problem. Here we demonstrate a deterministic method
  for integrating two deterministically created silicon self-interstitials with
  deterministically fabricated stress membrane nanomechanical resonators in silicon.
  Using advanced imaging methods, we imaged the proximity of the resonators to
  the self-interstitials and simulated the resonator-defect interaction to
  identify a new resonance shift mechanism induced by the defects that can be
  observed in Raman spectroscopy. This work provides a foundation for
  determining the unique defects-specific resonance shift and for controlling
  light-matter interactions with deterministically created defects in bulk silicon.

the brain is

  often yields inconsistent results, largely due to the high dimensionality and
  non-stationary nature of the data collected from fMRI scans. In this study, we

  accurately discern the functional connectivity between areas of the brain. We

  sensitivity to sparse and weak connections compared to traditional methods.

  all agents have access to the same reward signal, which is not the case in
  scenarios with sparse or localized rewards where each agent's reward is
  independent of other agents' actions.  Such environments with locally
  focused rewards pose a challenge for (meta-)learning generalizable policies
  in games that do not conform to typical learning conditions.  To investigate
  this issue, we explore whether generalizable policies can be learned in such
  non-conforming settings and provide a theoretical analysis of the impact of
  the reward distribution on sample complexity and algorithm performance.  Our
  analysis focuses on cooperative two-player games with finite state spaces and
  reveals a relationship between the generalizability of value functions and the
  mixing conditions of the reward distribution, establishing both sufficient
  and necessary conditions for learnability.  Ultimately, our work sheds light
  on the fundamental challenges of learning generalizable policies in sparse-
  reward multi-agent games.

This progress has motivated us to explore unsupervised video representation using self-supervised methods in a more complex setting: the domain shift scenario. In this specific context, we train models on large, unlabeled datasets from a source domain and evaluate them on smaller, targeted datasets from a target domain that contains specific classes of interest. This process typically involves collecting extensive, carefully annotated labeled data from the target domain, which can be time-consuming and costly. In contrast, our approach utilizes models that are pre-trained on massive, self-supervised foundations and fine-tunes them with limited data from the target domain. Our comparative analysis reveals the superiority of our method over existing alternatives and demonstrates the advantage of leveraging massive, unlabeled data from a domain that is different from the target domain, as well as the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

  These methods, however, have significant limitations, as they necessitate the collection of a substantial amount of data from each user, an impractical requirement.  To address this issue, we introduce a novel set of objectives that model each user as a single node and leverage their interactions with other nodes to predict their new connections.  These user-centric objectives can be implemented efficiently with minimal user data, such as up to 50 new connections per user.  We integrate these objectives into a bipartite graph neural network framework, initializing node and user representations separately and using a single shared graph neural network to predict the new connections for both.  We evaluate our approach on two large-scale datasets and demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms user-centered baselines while also surpassing the state-of-the-art bias-aware methods that do not require as much user data.  We also show that our approach achieves better results compared to the state-of-the-art bias-aware methods, even when trained with just one shared representation and approximately 100 seed connections, highlighting the effectiveness of our method with limited user data.

solid under high pressure is a fundamental challenge in condensed matter physics.  Although ab initio methods can accurately predict the ground state energy and total energy, using the Hamiltonian to study highly pressurized solids remains difficult.  To overcome this, we present a technique for constructing the high-pressure Hamiltonian from ab initio calculations using a quantum Monte Carlo solver, specifically for a system like hydrogen under extreme pressure.  Our approach recasts the DFT ground state energy as an effective potential within a path integral formulation, enabling us to derive a gauge-invariant, density-driven Hamiltonian that replicates the QMC ground state energy and total stress at the DFT level for that system.  As a practical application, we build such a Hamiltonian for normal hydrogen under high pressure, leveraging both fixed-node and diffusion hydrogen DFT calculations.  Our resulting Hamiltonian faithfully reproduces the DFT ground state energy, total stress, and density within 0.1%, 0.5%, and 0.5%, respectively, providing a starting point for more in-depth studies, such as examining phase transitions through perturbation theory.

the Prisoner's Dilemma framework, which is at the heart of numerous societal issues, including global warming and the spread of infectious diseases. In real-life situations involving social dilemmas, individuals' decisions are influenced by the actions of others to some extent. To account for the diverse range of human behavior in such scenarios, agent-based models are employed, in which a population of agents with varying personalities is created. This research investigates the outcomes of an agent-based simulation, where the agents exhibit the personalities described by the 'Big Five' model, within a Prisoner's Dilemma game. As a result, extant literature on this topic is expanded. Our simulation results, in which agents engage in a single round of the game, reveal distinct differences in average payoffs among the different personalities. Not surprisingly, Narcissists and Selfish individuals produce the worst outcomes for themselves and others, while Generous individuals achieve the best results. However, our findings concerning Neutrals and Anxieties are unexpected. In a subsequent experiment, we explore how the influence of Anxieties and Neutrals can be minimized to optimize collective outcomes in situations involving a solitary interaction.

Analyzing OCTA data to understand and diagnose various eye conditions is crucial, but this can be a time-consuming and tedious task for ophthalmologists. To expedite this process, optical coherence tomography angiography semantic segmentation (OCTA-SS) has emerged as an automated method to assign functional labels to pixels in retinal OCTA scans. To address these shortcomings, this study introduces a novel approach to OCTA semantic segmentation using the Lightly Supervised Joint Feature Learning (LSJFL) framework, an adaptive method that optimizes retinal OCTA feature learning through the collaboration of ophthalmologists and artificial intelligence. The results of this study indicate that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods on two distinct retinal OCTA datasets while being more efficient in terms of computational resources. The network flow reliability evaluation problem involves calculating the probability that at least 'k' paths between a starting point and an ending point are not obstructed. The problem becomes exponentially more complex when multiple origins and destinations are involved. We propose a novel approach to efficiently evaluate reliability in large-scale networks by developing an algorithm to generate all possible 'k-path combinations' between specific nodes and implementing the Monte Carlo simulation method for accurate estimation. The algorithm leverages the concept of implicit objects and utilizes an adapted version of the implicit 'k-ary tree' rule to develop the next 'k-path combination' from a previous one. A detailed examination of the algorithm's time requirements and the implementation of the implicit enumeration algorithm are discussed. Three test cases are used to compare the performance of the proposed approach to existing methods.

It's demonstrated that the required conditions can be met, with this possibility significantly broadened for heteronuclear combinations due to their larger interaction strength.  Notably, the Mott-insulator state characterizing Rabi resonances involves a species-specific pattern that can be shifted by varying the system's parameters, allowing access to an extensive range of patterns.  A key feature of the two-species system is its ability to exist as Rabi self-organized states that combine superfluid mobility enabling the formation of diverse patterns with self-trapping of each atom type in optical traps, resulting in a highly flexible system.  A theoretical model based on the Gross-Pitaevskii equations provides an effective description of Rabi self-organization and is validated through simulations of optical lattice manipulations supported by numerical simulations based on the full many-body Hamiltonian.

maintaining the stability and performance of closed-loop systems with input and state constraints, particularly in applications involving rigorous safety requirements.  The sum-and-sos (SOS) framework has gained significant interest in this field due to its tractable nature and ability to handle non-convex problems through conservatism.  However, utilizing SOS in fault-tolerant control poses computational challenges, as it necessitates the solution of a series of SOS optimization problems to determine a stabilizing control policy.  This paper presents a novel and finite set of closed-form feedback control laws that ensures constraint satisfaction and closed-loop stability for second-order strictly passive nonlinear systems subject to actuator faults.  Specifically, we develop a set of nested saturations-based feedback control laws parameterized by a Lyapunov-based barrier function, which guarantees state and input constraint satisfaction and asymptotic stability of the closed-loop system for a class of actuator faults.  To avoid the Zeno phenomenon, the proposed control laws are shown to be robust to disturbances within an explicit bound.  Furthermore, this paper introduces a finite set of switched overapproximating barrier certificates (SOBCs) that validates the closed-loop system's performance without resorting to exhaustive optimization.  The efficacy of the proposed control laws is demonstrated through numerical simulations of a DC motor and an underactuated robotic arm.

  $1/D$-quantized Hall states and critical phenomena beyond Lifshitz and
  Wilson-Fowler fixed points are widely regarded as some of theoretical
  physics' most captivating areas.  This research investigates the phase
  diagram of a generic, interacting $(2+1)$D system characterized by complex,
  multi-band symmetries and particle-hole conservation.  Our analysis employs
  variational methods to both explore this system's topological phases and
  assess its critical behavior.  This approach enables us to differentiate
  between essential and incidental aspects of these phenomena.  Our discoveries
  show that $(2+1)$D systems can support various types of highly-entangled states,
  such as $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and $\mathbb{Z}_3$ spin liquids, as well as $\mathbb{Z}_4$ and
  $\mathobel_3$ quantum double models.  Moreover, we demonstrate the existence of
  continuous transitions that follow the Dirac critical points and multiple,
  bi-stable topological phases within this framework.  This outcome implies
  that such scenarios are prevalent in $(2+1)$D systems with interacting
  electron-like particles, potentially enabling diverse topological phases like
  non-Abelian semions and anyons with higher charges.

By recruiting participants with no musical training and exposing them to the sound of a complex musical composition, researchers compared these inexperience listeners' responses to the music with their responses to a set of abstract concepts known to all humans.  The results revealed that inexperience listeners' brains processed the music in a similar manner to how the concept of time is understood.  Furthermore, it was discovered that the brain's processing of the temporal aspects of both music and the time concept activates the same neural regions, specifically those involved in representing time.  In contrast, it was found that the spatial aspects of both music and the time concept activate different areas of the brain, with listeners with no musical training perceiving the music as primarily rooted in the temporal domain, in line with existing research on the spatial-temporal characteristics of music.

  commonly referred to as intrinsic parton correlations beyond the leading 
  twist approximation. These correlations are intimately connected to 
  hadron's orbital motion of partons, which can be quantified through 
  parton GPDs and T-odd PDFs. As such, intrinsic parton correlations 
  play a significant role in various hadron processes, including diffractive 
  hadron production, particle production in fusion, and parton's orbital 
  motion influence on parton partner scattering. This can result in 
  asymmetries in cross sections. Recently, it has been proposed that 
  b-symmetry in final states, typically observed in exclusive final states, 
  may originate from parton intrinsic correlations, a phenomenon referred 
  as the recoil effect. This research paper provides a theoretical 
  framework for parton intrinsic correlations in the context of the 
  $K\pi\pi^0$ final state in the reaction $\bar{p}p\to K\pi\pi^0\mathcal{X}$, 
  suggesting that the observed $b$-symmetry in cross sections can serve as 
  a direct indication of parton intrinsic correlations, offering an 
  opportunity to study this phenomenon experimentally at the Fermilab 
  Main Injector.

AMV) is a decadal-scale climate pattern in the
  North Atlantic Ocean, which can influence the occurrence of La Niña and El Niño
  phenomena, as well as affect global weather patterns. Understanding the mechanisms
  behind AMV is crucial, especially considering its potential impact on climate
  variability on a multidecadal scale. In this study, we investigate AMV using a
  comprehensive coupled climate model, and identify two primary modes of variability
  in the North Atlantic Ocean - an interannual mode, which is similar to the
  Atlantic Niño, and an AMV mode, which is driven by a positive feedback loop
  resulting from the impact of sea surface temperature anomalies on thermohaline
  circulation. Additionally, El Niño and La Niña events in the model are
  triggered by the Atlantic variability through the ocean's adjustment to a
  thermohaline circulation mode, which is sustained by wind stress curl anomalies
  generated by the ENSO feedback mechanism of the ocean-atmosphere system. Our
  findings provide new insights into the complex interactions between AMV and ENSO,
  and have implications for the occurrence and prediction of these phenomena in
  the coming decades.

However, the reliance on pre-trained knowledge poses a risk when the injected knowledge is misleading, a situation that can occur frequently given the openness of web data sources.  Although several strategies have been proposed to mitigate the negative impact of such contaminated knowledge, they often necessitate supplementary training resources.  In this work, we introduce the concept of "defensive one-shot learning" (DOL), aiming to enable models to swiftly acquire correct knowledge from a single labeled example without necessitating extra training resources. The aim of this work is to explore the application of contextual information in processing compound words, a task that has received far less attention compared to its application in addressing word ambiguity.  To achieve this, a series of three experiments was conducted, each with its own unique approach and focus.  The first experiment involved the development of a binary classification model to distinguish between acceptable and unacceptable compound words, utilizing both the semantic compatibility of the constituent words and a vector-based representation of the entire compound word.  The second experiment involved the prediction of the initial word in a two-word compound word, using data from the Swatch corpus, and the third involved the completion of incomplete compound words in the same dataset.  The results indicated that the findings for the first experiment diverged from those for the second and third experiments in terms of the relative importance of the constituent words' features.  The experiments also demonstrated the effectiveness of a contextual learning approach in handling the comprehension of compound words, an outcome that is in contrast to the well-documented role of the first constituent word in the interpretation of ambiguous words.  The results obtained in this study may provide a valuable foundation for addressing the challenges associated with the interpretation of compound nouns in natural language processing tasks, such as part-of-speech tagging and the comprehension of incomplete compound words.

We identify and examine a defect in a topological insulator that can exist at the surface of bulk heterostructures composed of mercury telluride and cadmium selenide. This surface defect has a unique property of having no energy gap on the surface. arvesting potential in two-dimensional topological insulators remains a topic of debate.  To shed light on this issue, our study combines theoretical calculations with experimental data, comparing the energy at different frequencies in the Drude model and in experimental measurements.  The agreement between the two validates our findings, which also take into account the finite life-time of carriers and the relationship between the energy gap and carrier life-time.  The results show that the finite-energy flow occurs within the energy gap, with the exact range depending on the material properties, and that the maximum of the energy flow corresponds to the ratio of the carrier life-time to the energy gap.  The energy flow is non-zero at very low-temperatures, and its behavior at room-temperatures is non-monotonic, with an associated optimum temperature.  Our energy-harvesting protocol is valid at both room-temperatures and very low-temperatures, and could be applied to generate power in photovoltaic devices and in mechanical vibrations that are converted to electrical energy through time-varying strain.  The protocol is general and is not limited to the specific material studied, which is HgTe quantum wells, and energy flow is observed for a wide range of topological materials at both very low and room temperatures.

The success of CNNs is impeded by several key challenges, including their excessive parameter count, poor performance on patched or patchified data, and their poor generalization capabilities.  The proliferation of pruning techniques has facilitated the development of lightweight CNN architectures, yet their efficiency is severely compromised when paired with the necessity for them to function effectively on patchified data.  The concept of complete invariance to any form of data patching has long been regarded as elusive.  The work of Complementary Pruning Convolutional Neural Networks (Complementary-PCNNs) introduces a novel, mutually complementary and complementary-pruned CNN model, which has been shown to exhibit complete invariance to data patching. In order to detect non-point-like behavior in quarks, researchers assessed the production rates of new particle resonances decaying into quark pairs as a function of the momentum transfer involved in the interaction. A new particle resonance has a point-like interaction characteristic, however such behavior is altered in quarks with chromoelectric charge. Interaction strength is affected in this scenario at high momentum transfers, allowing the effective charge of quarks to be derived from data for various final states. solar corona is best described by an advection-diffusion equation, where the level of non-ohmic resistance varies significantly with altitude.  A key insight is that a critical threshold exists, beyond which magnetic flux can escape the well-guided state and is rapidly dispersed.  A new framework is proposed to estimate the altitude where this escape occurs, utilizing fast CME initiation models.  It is argued that the initial conditions for these models, specifically the distribution of magnetic flux, can be derived from potential field extrapolations using slow reconnection.  This overestimate of the guiding force results in an elevated threshold altitude, which, if set to the corona's base, would imply near-perfect magnetic guidance and extremely long reconnection timescales, effectively rendering CMEs impossible.  A reduction in the threshold altitude to around 5-10 Mm from the photosphere, however, leads to more realistic reconnection timescales of around 1-10 hours.  This decreased threshold altitude also explains the observed spread in CMEs on the solar disk, as well as the delay between solar flares and CMEs, and suggests that the flaring process occurs above the photosphere.

Ensuring the reliability of such critical decisions requires a deep understanding of the factors that influence an system's behavior.  Recent studies have shown that standard machine learning models often rely on spurious correlations, which can lead to poor performance when encountered in real-world settings.  Despite this, current fairness evaluations still use trained models as proxies, potentially reinforcing these associations.  This research reveals that such models exhibit significant variability in their fairness metrics when tested on real datasets, and the root cause is the development of low-confidence areas that differ between demographic groups.  As a result, the labeled data present in the test sets may not accurately reflect the system's true fairness.  To address this issue, we propose GCPQ, a method that estimates the most probable fairness gap based on the model's confusion between protected classes within its low-confidence regions.  Our study demonstrates GCPQ's accuracy in estimating fairness gaps and explores the model's decision-making process from this perspective, uncovering the underlying causes of such metrics' variability.  Ultimately, GCPQ offers a more informed approach to assessing the reliability and ethical implications of real-world machine learning models.

  generative model for optimizing node evaluations within the MCTC framework.  We
  have successfully applied this algorithm to two card games: 1) The cooperative

  nonlocal objects, including wormholes and branes in various theories of 
  gravity and scalar fields.  Possible nonlocality in gravitational and 
  scalar field systems is closely linked to time noncausality and 
  chronology violations.  Chronologically and thermodynamically 
  reasonable conditions place constraints on the nonlocality of such 
  objects, with their nonlocality becoming more pronounced in the 
  microcanonical limit and in scenarios involving white holes and 
  white branes.  In the case of wormholes, the quantum evolution of 
  internal clocks indicates that the distance within them is imaginary, 
  reflecting the inherent nonlocality of these objects.  In contrast, 
  the evolution of clock fields within branes suggests that their 
  nonlocality can be quantified in terms of their internal clock time.

We investigate the thermodynamics associated with drive-and-measure quantum processes that reach cyclic steady states, utilizing generalized thermal states known as Gibbs states for SNEQ thermodynamics.  It has been established that the cyclic free energy difference between two distinct quantum engines depends on the thermodynamics of the steady states.  We develop a method to calculate the cyclic free energy difference utilizing the characteristic function of the weak measurement, and we utilize this to determine the Gibbs state for both bosonic and fermionic SNEQ systems. on resource-constrained IoT devices poses significant challenges, stemming from the time-consuming training and inference processes.  To tackle this issue, Crowdsourced Federated Learning (CFL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for jointly optimizing system resources and coordinating multiple learners to collaborate on collaborative models.  However, the complex CFL orchestration is further complicated by the intermittent and variable connectivity of mobile networks, posing significant challenges in real-world deployments.  In this study, we introduce an Optimal Coordination Algorithm (OCA) that formulates the CFL problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) to optimally determine orchestration variables and minimize energy consumption.  We present an Enhanced OCA (EOCA) algorithm that incorporates CFL feature selection and data subset selection to improve system efficiency and model performance.  Our simulations, based on a real-world IoT dataset, indicate that EOCC outperforms OCA and the baseline algorithms in terms of energy efficiency, data subset selection, model accuracy, and F1-score.

have proven highly effective in various network-related tasks, but their robustness against adversarial attacks remains a significant concern.  Current research into the robustness of GNNs primarily centers on designing and analyzing defensive mechanisms and models.  In contrast, this work takes a novel approach by investigating the inherent properties of GNN algorithms that could inadvertently facilitate adversarial model manipulation.  Our analysis reveals that the inherent design of GNN algorithms can be exploited to create a backdoor, specifically, a short path between the backdoor and target nodes remains undetected during data processing, leading to the misclassification of unseen inputs.  Based on this insight, we propose a straightforward backdoor injection technique called RAMP, which leverages the inherent properties of GNN algorithms to insert a short path between backdoor and target nodes, and can effectively trigger the backdoor without requiring additional parameters or altering the original model structure.  Furthermore, RAMP exhibits high efficiency and scalability, enabling the insertion of numerous backdoors between multiple node pairs with minimal label requirements and high success rates across different types of adversarial attacks.  Finally, our comprehensive experiments demonstrate the high effectiveness and versatility of RAMP in inserting multiple backdoors across various types of graphs and neural network architectures.

This paper introduces Ethos, a precise warning system for detecting common security issues in a vast portion of Ethereum's most used libraries.  By building on the capabilities of Solvers, Ethos can identify specific security issues such as re-entrancy, where an attacker can recursively call a function for profit, and unchecked return values, which can lead to failed transactions with valuable assets.  In contrast to previous methods, Ethos doesn't get stuck solving incorrect paths and is able to check the safety of code with obfuscated ownership transfers.  The precision of Ethos is demonstrated through its ability to verify the safety of over 70,000 Ethereum transactions with complex protection features.  The effectiveness of Ethos is shown by its capacity to discover multiple unpatched bugs in well-known libraries and even replicate attacker behavior in one instance, causing a loss of 165,000 ETH. The effectiveness of Ethos is shown with a 70-fold improvement in solver speed and the ability to analyze code with dynamic feature that was unavailable before.

high accuracy and low bias. A model's high accuracy is typically evaluated using standard metrics on benchmark datasets, while its low bias is assessed through diverse classification distribution analysis. However, these evaluation methods often focus solely on either accuracy or bias, neglecting the importance of both. A model's performance on benchmark datasets is a common indicator of its low bias, but this does not necessarily mean the model's classification distribution is similarly balanced. Conversely, models with similar classification distributions may exhibit varying levels of accuracy. To address this limitation, we first introduce a metric to quantify models' similar classification distributions, and propose an ensemble-based approach to measure models' similar biased distribution. This method evaluates the extent to which a model's similar biased distribution influences its accuracy, and in return, assesses the model's accuracy as an indicator of its similar biased distribution. A model's similar biased distribution is influenced by multiple factors, and this influence differs from model to model.

intense emissions from gamma rays associated with the collapse of massive stars or the merger of compact objects. As these events often involve relativistic jets, the structure of these jets significantly impacts their observed properties. Focusing on the most intense part of the spectrum, we investigate how viewing the burst at different angles relative to its axis of symmetry results in distinct temporal patterns. Our Monte Carlo simulations, which consider multiple emission components, also account for the Doppler effect and integrate the burst's total intensity. The outcome reveals a universal time delay formula, allowing us to determine the most intense time of the burst based on the viewing angle and the jet's density profile. This, in turn, allows us to determine the arrival time difference between bursts observed on the burst's axis and those seen at an offset angle, which should be possible to detect with future high-sensitivity gamma-ray telescopes. By comparing our theoretical predictions with actual GRB observations, we can potentially determine the structure of GRB jets.

learning models relies on the the technique of fine-tuning, which is the process of retraining the model on a smaller, specialized dataset.  As an alternative, we present a strategy that involves a single, pre-trained model handling both the tasks of generalization and the task of personalization.  Our method, based on a new mathematical framework, involves introducing a new term to the model's loss function that serves as a penalty for deviating from the pre-trained model's output.  By formulating this problem using a smooth min function, the model can be trained with a single optimization step.  Our research indicates a crucial finding, which is that a certain threshold must be met in terms of the pre-trained model's accuracy on a specific data point in order for the model to be effectively personalized.  If this threshold is not be met, the new method converges to the traditional fine-tuning solution.  To address this limitation, we propose a new technique that is capable of overcoming this threshold and pave the way for a range of custom strategies.  We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on the tasks of image classification and web search query classification, achieving superior results to the conventional fine-tuning approach.
