Action Recognition, fast
  methods often sacrifice accuracy. Conversely, the most accurate models are
  computationally complex and prohibitively slow. Typically, researchers train
  models on datasets like ImageNet and then prune them to reduce computation
  time. However, this practice often degrades their pruning performance. In
  Action Recognition, we aim to prune deep networks to achieve (1) quicker
  inference and (2) comparable or improved accuracy to state-of-the-art fast
  baselines. To this end, we introduce a novel pruning technique called Coarse-to
  Fine Pruning (C2F-Pruning). C2F-Pruning starts by training a network on a
  smaller dataset (e.g., IMNET) and progressively transfers it to networks with
  increasingly larger feature sets and a coarser downsampling pattern, ultimately
  achieving (1) reduced inference time and (2) enhanced accuracy. To our
  advantage, C2F-Pruning can employ larger feature networks, leading to better
  performance. To test our pruning framework, we utilize three popular networks
  (ResNet, ResNeSt, and SE-ResNet) and achieve significant improvements in
  (1) final accuracy and (2) minimum computation time. C2F-Pruning results are
  available at
  https://sites.google.com/view/c2f-pruning/home.

release is a privacy-preserving approach that

  notion of DP can have a significant impact on the properties of the released
  data, potentially distorting correlations and relationships present in the
  original data. As a result, a DP dataset released to the public may be
  insufficient for certain downstream machine learning tasks. Although various
  techniques have been developed to learn effective models from private datasets,
  they are typically applied after the data has been collected. In contrast, this
  work aims to incorporate a privacy component into a broader data pipeline,
  proposing a unified pipeline for learning private machine learning models that
  preserves model performance and satisfies DP guarantees. Specifically, this work
  introduces a novel approach called the Data Transformation Module (DTM), an
  adaptive module that transforms a private dataset to facilitate effective
  modeling. The DTM can be integrated into existing machine learning pipelines,
  enhancing them with a privacy-preserving component. Through careful design, the
  DTM can adapt to various machine learning models, such as Random Forests and
  Neural Networks, and can be fine-tuned to balance the trade-off between model
  performance and DP guarantees. Our comprehensive data-driven approach has been
  thoroughly evaluated on three real-world datasets and consistently demonstrates
  improved machine learning model performance compared to baseline private
  learning methods.

remote sensing, a data-driven approach is being developed, known as weakly-supervised learning.  This learning type is uniquely positioned to handle remotely sensed data that has been partially labeled, which is cost-effective to acquire and process.  Unfortunately, the high degree of label freedom associated with weak labels often complicates the interpretation of results and limits their utility for real-world applications.  To address this challenge, a cutting-edge method for weakly-supervised semantic segmentation has been developed, which utilizes comparatively inexpensive but more interpretable constraints called multi-instance constraints.  This new framework integrates the popular 2D convolutional neural network architecture, called Mask R-CNN, with the goal of addressing the weakly-supervised semantic segmentation task under multi-instance constraints.  A novel learning strategy has been devised to teach the network to predict pixel-level labels, while simultaneously minimizing the discrepancy between predicted labels and actual annotations within the positive bag associated with each image.  Additionally, a novel masking strategy has been formulated to iteratively refine the segmentation mask by selectively masking and retraining the network on the current mask and newly generated but distinct samples until convergence is achieved.  Experiments conducted on the MS COCO dataset have demonstrated the effectiveness of this method in improving the interpretability of weakly-supervised semantic segmentation and achieving competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art methods.

This study aims to enhance certification radii by utilizing multi-linear approximations similar to the TRM method. Differentiating from the original TRM, this work proposes an alternative multi-linear approximation in the form of a convex envelope, which it names ELIOT. In contrast to neural networks' generally non-convex nature, the certification problem involves minimizing a convex function within a convex set, allowing the development of an exact convex approximation of a neural network's convex under-estimator, which surpasses previous limitations. A key innovation, the Soft-Max Partitioning function, effectively substitutes the non-differentiable convex maximum operation with an efficiently computable and parameterizable approximation. Through the integration of this function into a variational approach, a tightly fitting convex under-estimator of neural networks can be derived, which can be utilized for computing larger certified $L_\infty$ and $L_\infty + L_2$ robustness regions. Furthermore, a novel branch-and-bound algorithm tailored for the maximization of the proposed convex approximation of the neural network's lower approximation has been developed, which demonstrates a significant improvement in certified robustness regions in experiments on the MNIST and EMNIST datasets in comparison to existing methods.

Beam-dynamics restrictions such as longitudinal emgrowth and the onset of electron cloud formation are crucial considerations when designing and optimizing the final stages of such accelerators. Through thorough measurements and subsequent analysis at the Large Hadron Collider's injection energy, the underlying causes of emgrowth in the LHC's main ring were investigated. However, the potential of these systems is hindered by a lack of effective methods to program memristive crossbar arrays and update their stored knowledge.  This paper presents a programming and programming update algorithm that programs and updates the arrays in a time-efficient and time-constrained manner and in a three-stages manner manner.  First, the target array is partitioned into sub-arrays that share the same input and/or target values.  Then, the sub-arrays are sequentially programmed in a time-constrained manner, and the time-efficient update is achieved by programs multiple variants of a sub-array and switching between the variants by reconfiguring the surrounding multiplexers.  The proposed algorithm is verified by computer simulation and implemented in FPGAs, and the results show that it significantly improves the programming and update time compared to the existing methods, and that it can effectively exploit the inherent characteristics of STT-MRAM and SRAM to achieve fast reconfiguration.

The gravitational wave signal from the phase transition can be amplified in the ULAP phase, prior to the phase transition's end, due to ULAP's unique properties of a non-zero pressure, high sound speed, and prolonged phase transition duration. To address these challenges, we have created the RankRecs framework, a (open-source) tool that facilitates the accurate and efficient evaluation of recommender systems. This framework is designed to be user-friendly and can be incorporated into research projects to produce reliable performance metrics. To showcase its capabilities, we have utilized RankRecs to generate the Oxford University Recommender Systems Benchmark, a publicly available benchmark that is incorporated into the (open-source) OUDS platform.

The problem is ill-posed as it can either lack a solution or exhibit significant sensitivity to data noise.  The study is set in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with Neumann boundary conditions, though the findings are applicable to $\mathbb{R}^d$. The assumption of piecewise smooth source terms may be relaxed to encompass a broader class of functions. ability of data augmentation is still an open question.  Generalization can be modeled as a form of regularization that regularizes the network to be invariant to the augmented transformations.  This perspective suggests that the purpose of data augmentation is to regularize the network with the loss function, which in turn indicates that the network should learn features that are invariant to the augmented transformations for the optimal performance.  However, in practice, it is very hard to regularize the network with a loss function that explicitly requires the network to be invariant.  In contrast, random data augmentation has a different effect - it randomizes the size of the neural network by a certain degree, which has a similar effect as network dropout.  This randomization of the size of the neural network has a similar purpose as dropout - to regularize the network and to prevent the network from overfitting.  This paper theoretically and experimentally validates the randomization hypothesis.  A key finding from our analysis is that random data augmentation increases the variance of the Jacobian matrix, which indicates that the randomization hypothesis is more aligned with the mathematical properties of the problem at hand.  Furthermore, our experiments show that many data augmentation techniques that perform well in visual recognition tasks are effective in randomizing the size of the neural network by a certain degree, which in turn leads to better generalization performance.  This randomization hypothesis also provides a simple and effective framework for designing new data augmentation techniques that can lead to novel insights and significant performance improvements.

The study expands on this concept by considering graphs that are generated with varying degrees of randomness. The topology of a particular set of graphs, denoted as $\cal G$, in relation to a given countable group, $\Gamma$, can determine the ability of a randomly mapped element of the group to generate the entire group as a subgroup. The map from $\Gamma$ to each individual graph in $\cal G$ is required to be a homomorphism. The research proves that if the topology of $\cal G$ is in relation to a product of the graph where $\Gamma$ is mapped to itself, then the random endomorphism of a free $\Gamma$-tree has a strong automorphism property. The result also provides an alternative proof for a previous theorem by Schramm and van der Zwaan regarding the random normal covering of a countable free group. The question is raised as to whether the condition placed on the topology of $\cal G$ can be relaxed.

In contrast, some networks exhibit specific topological features that lead to exceptional properties, such as the spectral gap in regular graphs and the isolation of community structures in modular networks. Here, we investigate how a network's random dynamics are impacted by its topological characteristics, focusing on the spectral gap and community structure. We demonstrate that a spectral gap can accelerate node deactivation within a single cluster but simultaneously hasten node dissemination across community boundaries. Similarly, we reveal that clearly defined community structures slow down node dissemination but hasten node deactivation within communities. Ultimately, our findings underscore the necessity of considering network topology when assessing the efficiency of epidemic spreading.

Wittenberg first described the local Galois representations associated with a classical modular form at prime 2. At a prime p other than 2, if the form has rational coefficients, its local Galois representations can be found at nearly all 2 if and only if the form displays certain symmetries at 2 in a certain way. This paper aims to investigate the converse statement at 2. If a newform displays certain non-exceptional modular symmetry types and has integer coefficients at 2, then there exists a modular representation that matches the form's local symmetries at 2 at 2 infinite places.

We find that the scalar field's influence on the signal prior to the late-phase is minimal, except when the binary approaches close proximity to coalescence. We explore the ejection of the scalar field during the merger and its ability to induce quasi-bound states around the remnant black hole, which in turn can produce a detectable gravitational wave signal lasting several hundred milliseconds. We also investigate the possibility of the scalar field inducing a phase transition in the universe and suggest that a future detector with high sensitivity may be able to place constraints on this process and on other possible processes produced by the scalar field during the merger.
